source.title: DPlis: Boosting Utility of Differentially Private Deep Learning via Randomized Smoothing
source.authors: Wen-Xiao Wang; Tian-Hao Wang; Lun Wang; Nanqing Luo; Pan Zhou; D. Song; R. Jia

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies whether smoothing the training loss improves generalization and stability in differentially private training, using test performance and a sharpness measure. Its DP-SGD setup differs from the claim's standard-training settings.
record.gate_note: The paper's results concern randomized smoothing for DP-SGD and PATE. They do not test the listed natural-label, non-private versions. Table 9 measures sharpness, but does not compare generalization gaps among networks trained to similarly low training loss.
record.test_reason: Table 2 tests V3 in a new setting: CNNs and fully connected MLPs trained from scratch with DP-SGD on MNIST and CIFAR-10. CNNs have higher test accuracy at every reported privacy budget, both without smoothing and with smoothing. Differential privacy does not make this architecture comparison irrelevant. The sharpness results do not test V7's relationship with generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that smoothing improves DP-SGD utility and performance stability, derive a generalization bound that improves with training-loss smoothness under their assumptions, and demonstrate utility improvements when extending smoothing to PATE.
record.recipe_differences: Uses DP-SGD with per-example gradient clipping and added Gaussian noise; the intervention smooths the loss by averaging over parameter perturbations. The paper also evaluates a PATE extension.
record.method_sensitivity: Smoothing radius changes performance; the authors describe performance as approximately unimodal in R. Larger K generally improves performance in the two settings tested for K.

fits_no_version.finding: Randomized smoothing reduces reported sharpness in all four architecture–dataset comparisons in Table 9.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Randomized smoothing guides DP-SGD toward solutions with lower measured local sharpness.

fits_no_version.finding: CIFAR-10 MLP test performance declines during vanilla DP-SGD without an increasing generalization gap; training performance also declines.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Declining test performance during DP-SGD can reflect deteriorating training performance rather than increasing overfitting.

record.problems: The main accuracy tables report single-run results. Stability is evaluated across five runs for only selected settings. Sharpness measurements do not directly test whether sharpness tracks generalization gaps.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results left out; the paper's accuracy tables report DP utility rather than a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width-dependent test error beyond the interpolation threshold.
The contribution of local connectivity, learned sparse connections, and initialization from a trained convolutional network.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning regimes.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Dropout effects and interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Whether magnitude-aware sharpness ranks generalization gaps among networks with similarly low training loss, including comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples.

missing.what: Matched CNN-versus-MLP test-accuracy comparisons on MNIST and CIFAR-10 at privacy budgets 1.99, 5.01, 7.01, and 10.00, separately for no smoothing, R = 10, and R = Rbest. These directly bear on V3 despite the record's dismissal of the accuracy tables as only DP utility results.
missing.locator: Sections 5.1–5.2; Table 2; smoothing-radius choices in Table 6

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V3. Its CNN–MLP comparisons support the accuracy ordering in private training but do not isolate local connectivity as its cause. Table 9 and the generalization theorem concern different quantities from V7's empirical ranking of generalization gaps.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; the listed architectures, training recipes, and datasets.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD, including tuning and weight-decay conditions.
Large versus small batch training under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
The paper reports sharpness values and test performance under DP-SGD, but does not measure whether magnitude-aware sharpness ranks generalization gaps among networks with similarly low training loss.
Removing memorized examples and comparing test accuracy with random-example removal.

rows.measure: Whether the generalization gap increased as test performance degraded
rows.value: The paper states that no increasing generalization gap was observed.
rows.note: The text attributes the declining test performance primarily to declining training performance; exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The reported absence of an increasing generalization gap is accurate, but does not measure any listed version. Preserve that finding separately; 'absent' should not imply that a listed claim's effect is absent. The explanation appears in Section 5.4, with the initial observation in Section 5.2.

relationships.condition: MNIST and CIFAR-10; training from scratch with vanilla DP-SGD or DP-SGD with fixed smoothing radius R = 10; all four reported privacy budgets.
relationships.reason: Based on Table 2, missing from the rows: CNN test accuracy exceeds MLP accuracy in every matched comparison. Without smoothing, MNIST CNN accuracy is 95.08–96.07% versus 92.60–94.11% for MLPs; CIFAR-10 CNN accuracy is 49.70–61.37% versus 41.07–43.88%. The same ordering holds with R = 10.
relationships.display_finding: The reported higher CNN test accuracy at every privacy budget, without smoothing and with fixed smoothing, remains unverified.
